title: Variables referencing Lazily Imported modules load the modules
author: aneroid

text:
I feel like this is covered by the reification section of the PEP you mention:

Accessing a lazy object (from a global variable or a module attribute) reifies the object.
However, calling globals() or accessing a module’s __dict__ does not trigger reification – they return the module’s dictionary, and accessing lazy objects through that dictionary still returns lazy proxy objects that need to be manually reified upon use. A lazy object can be resolved explicitly by calling the resolve method. Calling dir() at the global scope will not reify the globals, nor will calling dir(mod) (through special-casing in mod.__dir__.) Other, more indirect ways of accessing arbitrary globals (e.g. inspecting frame.f_globals) also do not reify all the objects.

I suppose the term ‘accessing’ might lead people to think it’s when you touch some element of the lazy_import object itself but this isn’t the case. This is intended to mean when the name itself is looked up.
>>> lazy import json
>>> m = globals()['json']
>>> globals()['m']
<lazy_import 'json'>
>>> m  # Here m is accessed from a global variable and so is resolved and replaced
<module 'json' from '.../json/__init__.py'>

So type(m) is not the same as type(globals()['json']) because globals()['json'] is the lazy_module object while m is being looked up from a global variable and as such is resolved and replaced by the actual json module.
There’s some additional explanation for why globals() doesn’t resolve lazy imports near the end of the rejected ideas section.

One additional thing to note is that the lazy_import objects aren’t themselves converted into the resulting object. The lookup instead resolves the import and then replaces that name in the appropriate namespace. This means if you have another reference to the same lazy object that reference won’t be replaced.
>>> lazy import json
>>> m = globals()['json']
>>> globals()['m']
<lazy_import 'json'>
>>> globals()['m'] is globals()['json']
True
>>> m
<module 'json' from '.../json/__init__.py'>
>>> globals()['m'] is globals()['json']
False
>>> globals()['json']
<lazy_import 'json'>

text:
David Ellis:

I feel like this is covered by the reification section of the PEP you mention:


FWIW, in general, if something in Python can only be understood by reading the PEP, then we should update the documentation to explain it. PEPs are historical records of decision making.
The docs don’t need to explain all the rejected alternatives, but they should be enough to describe the implemented behavior.
The docs say:

The actual module is loaded on first use of that name.




 Anirudh D:

To me, it’s counterintuitive that type(globals()['json']) doesn’t load the module but type(m) does. Either both should or both shouldn’t. So it seems like a bug.


type(json) uses the Python name “json”. type(globals()['json']) doesn’t use the name “json”, it access the thing “json” refers to, through a different mechanism.



 Anirudh D:

My guess was that type(m) requires de-referencing m to find what object it points to (for lack of better Python terminology). And that act of de-referencing m also loads whatever m points to. But for type(globals()['json']), the type function already gets a reference to the lazy-module so it doesn’t get loaded. One of these is probably an exceptional case intentionally written into the Python interpreter.


I think you have the correct understanding.  How would you amend the sentence in the docs to make this clearer? I wouldn’t write a whole paragraph about it, since it’s getting into details of how Python names reference their values which isn’t particular to lazy imports.

Thing is, lazy imports don’t have similar behaviour with other things in Python. Not with weakrefs, descriptors, mutable objects (for dictionaries d1 = d2; assert d1 is d2), functions ( f = foo), etc. (Other places which have behaviours we learn about early on, usually in a code bug or a gotcha.)

That first result is similar to weakrefs but not the second. Using the weakref docs:
>>> import weakref
... class Object:
...     pass
...
>>> o1 = Object()
>>> r = weakref.ref(o1)
>>> o2 = r()
>>> o1 is o2
True
>>> # additionally
>>> r1 = weakref.ref(o1)
>>> r2 = weakref.ref(o1)  # also for o1
>>> r1 is r2
True

(That’s an example of the unfamiliarity of the behaviour of references to lazy imports.)

text:
Anirudh D:

I’d expect m to also have been a reference to a lazy module, and that type(m) would also return <class 'lazy_import'>


m is a reference to a lazy module. Writing:
lazy import json
m = globals()['json']

m is now a module attribute of type lazy_import. Whether it got there via lazy import or assignment is irrelevant at this point.
is essentially the same as
lazy import json
lazy import json as m

If instead of assigning to __main__.m you instead added it to a non-module container, it wouldn’t get reified:
>>> lazy import json
>>> m = [globals()['json']]
>>> m[0]
<lazy_import 'json'>
>>> type(m[0])
<class 'lazy_import'>
author: BenjyWiener

text:
Anirudh D:

Thing is, lazy imports don’t have similar behaviour with other things in Python. Not with weakrefs, descriptors, mutable objects (for dictionaries d1 = d2; assert d1 is d2), functions ( f = foo), etc. (Other places which have behaviours we learn about early on, usually in a code bug or a gotcha.)


It’s similar to accessing objects through a special __getattribute__ that checks for LazyImportType objects and resolves and replaces them. Pulling from __dict__ doesn’t resolve, while accessing as an attribute can and other references to the original object are left alone.
Here’s a rough emulation of what I mean:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from importlib import import_module
from pprint import pp
from types import SimpleNamespace

@dataclass
class FakeLazyImport:
    module_name: str

class FakeModule(SimpleNamespace):
    def __getattribute__(self, name):
        value = super().__getattribute__(name)
        if isinstance(value, FakeLazyImport):
            value = import_module(value.module_name)
            self.__setattr__(name, value)
        return value

fake_json = FakeLazyImport("json")

mod = FakeModule( 
    json=fake_json, 
)

mod.m = mod.__dict__["json"]
assert mod.__dict__["m"] is mod.__dict__["json"]
mod.m  # __getattribute__ triggered, m is replaced
pp(mod.__dict__)

{'json': FakeLazyImport(module_name='json'),
 'm': <module 'json' from '.../json/__init__.py'>}

The LazyImportType is special in that it has this behaviour when accessed as a global variable too.

text:
David Ellis:

To be clear this wasn’t intended as a gotcha. My intent was that it’s unfortunate for us as users of the documentation, not unfortunate for @nedbat that this is the case.


I know, but I still stand by my statement: this is the sort of straight-forward contribution that you, or anyone else who’s feeling bitten by this, can make. Start by proposing some new wording right here in this thread; if it looks good, you can make it into a pull request.
It IS unfortunate for readers of the documentation to have to go to the PEP. Those are, as Ned said, not intended to be living documents. When docs link to PEPs, we get update requests saying “the PEP isn’t how things are now” or “the PEP is out of date”, but that’s not what PEPs are for. They’re historical documents. Aside from fixing typos or broken links, we don’t want to be making major edits to them. That’s what documentation is for. Maybe initially, the docs can largely borrow from the language in the PEP; but the docs are a living document and will be edited as needed.
Note, by the way, that the license terms on PEPs are incredibly free (scroll down to the bottom of any PEP to see), so you are absolutely allowed to copy/paste text out of the PEP to make your documentation proposal.
